title: Lab 1 – Hypothalamus, pituitary, puberty
html:
Source: LP 1.pdf – 8 pages

Hypothalamus #1

  • MAGNOCELLULAR system-> neurosecretory granules (ADH and oxytocin) travel down the long
  • axons -> pituitary stalk-> posterior hypophysis (storage)-> release directly into the general
  • circulation
  • PARVOCELLULAR system-> hypophysiotropic hormones (GHRH, TRH, CRH, GnRH, dopamine,
  • somatostatin)-> secreted into the portal system-> pituitary stalk-> anterior hypophysis
  • (stimulate) GHRH-> GH; TRH-> TSH, PRL; CRH-> ACTH, MSH; GnRH-> FSH, LH
  • (inhibit) Dopamine-> PRL; Somatostatin-> GH, TSH
  • !! Hormones of the hypothalamus are secreted episodically, not continuously
  • !! Non-endocrine hypothalamic functions: body temperature, thirst, food intake, mood/
  • behavior, sleep, sex drive, activity of the autonomic system.
  • Pituitary gland- anatomy
  • - Located at the base of the skull in the sella turcica
  • - Covered by the diaphragm sellae (dural membrane with nervous endings)
  • - Linked to the hypothalamus through the pituitary stalk
  • - Lateral to gland- the cavernous sinuses (traversed by the III, IV, VI cranial nerves, the
  • ophthalmic branch of V cranial nerve, internal carotid arteries)
  • - Inferior to the gland- the sphenoid sinus
  • - Above the diaphragm sellae and anterior to the stalk- the optic chiasm
  • Pituitary gland- Main hormones
  • GH IGF-1 (mediator of the indirect actions of GH) and exerts direct actions on growth
  • and metabolism
  • PRL milk production (protein and lactose synthesis, water excretion, and sodium
  • retention)
  • gonadotropins secretion
  • ACTH glucocorticoids (zona fasciculata) and sex steroids (zona reticularis), hyperplasia
  • and hypertrophy of the adrenal cortex
  • TSH thyroid gland function (all aspects): hormone synthesis, secretion, hyperplasia,
  • hypertrophy, and vascularization

Pituitary gland- Main hormones #2

  • LH - F: ovulation induction
  • promotes luteinization, maintains the corpus luteum
  • synthesis of progesterone (corpus luteum) and androgens (theca interna cells)
  • - M : steroid hormones production (Leydig cells)
  • FSH - F: follicular development and estrogen and inhibin secretion ( granulosa cells)
  • -
  • M : spermatogenesis and inhibin secretion
  • OXYTOCIN contraction of the myoepithelial cells (mammary ducts)-> milk ejection
  • uterine contraction during labor
  • ADH - increases water permeability (collecting ducts)-> water reabsorption
  • - in higher concentrations-> pressor effect (vasoconstriction)
  • Regulation Mechanisms
  • A feedback mechanism is a loop in which a product feeds back to control its own production
  • 1. Negative feedback : high levels of an end-
  • product or negative regulator (inorganic
  • ion/metabolite/hormone) will initiate changes
  • which will decrease its production.
  • E.g.- hypercalcemia for PTH
  • - thyroid hormone for TSH
  • - IGF-1 for GH
  • - cortisol for ACTH
  • - hypoglycemia for insulin
  • 2. Positive feedback : positive regulator
  • stimulates hormone release
  • E.g. - In both childbirth and breastfeeding oxytocin additional release of oxytocin
  • - Mid-cycle estradiol-induced LH secretion
  • Types of endocrine disorders
  • Central (secondary or tertiary)- when the pituitary gland or the hypothalamus are affected
  • Primary (peripheral)- when the endocrine glands controlled by the HP axis are affected
  • Hormone-resistance syndromes (e.g. steroid, androgen or thyroid hormone receptor
  • resistance syndromes)-> clinical phenotype suggesting hormone deficiency
  • -> ↑ levels of circulating hormone
  • -> ↑ (or inappropriately detectable) levels of the relevant trophic
  • regulatory hormone (e.g., ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH).

The pituitary tumor syndrome-causes #3

  •  Pituitary adenomas (most of them are benign)- microadenoma (<1 cm in diameter)/
  • macroadenoma (>1 cm), nonfunctional pituitary adenoma/functional pituitary
  • adenomas (e.g. prolactinomas)
  •  Pituitary adenocarcinomas
  •  Craniopharyngiomas
  •  Metastatic lesions (breast/pulmonary/ GI cancer)
  •  Meningiomas, chordoma, glioma, cysts
  •  Granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, histiocytosis x)
  •  Lymphomas, leukemia, lymphocytic hypophysitis
  •  Pituitary abscesses
  • The pituitary tumor syndrome-clinical picture
  • Neurological signs and symptoms
  • Headache (stretching of the diaphragm sellae by a tumoral mass)
  • - frontal, frontoparietal or retro-orbital localization
  • - none/ only partial amelioration with the usual painkillers
  • - progressive in severity
  • - if the tumor erodes and drops into the sphenoid sinus-> the headache decreases in
  • severity+ CSF fluid leak
  • Hypothalamic syndrome (the evolution of pituitary masses toward the hypothalamus)
  • - hyperphagia and weight gain
  • - loss of thirst sensation
  • - diabetes insipidus
  • - somnolence
  • - problems with temperature control
  • - behavior changes
  • Neurological signs and symptoms
  • Signs and symptoms caused by extension into the cavernous sinus
  • - diplopia, palpebral ptosis, ophthalmoplegia
  • - internal carotid artery compression – cerebral circulatory insufficiency
  • - cavernous sinus thrombosis.
  • Increased intracranial pressure (very large tumors with both suprasellar and parasellar
  • extension) = NEUROSURGICAL EMERGENCY
  • - severe, persistent headache
  • - vomiting
  • - seizures
  • - bradycardia
  • - papillary edema

The pituitary tumor syndrome-clinical picture #4

  • Ophthalmological signs and symptoms = NEUROSURGICAL EMERGENCIES
  • The optic—chiasmatic syndrome (the tumor is impinging upon the optic chiasm or optic tract)
  • - bitemporal superior quadrantanopia (pressure on the inferior crossing chiasmatic
  • fibers which lead to bitemporal visual loss, in the superior field portions)
  • - bitemporal heteronymous hemianopia (all the crossing chiasmatic fibers are affected)
  • - homonymous contralateral hemianopia (tumor evolution toward an optic tract-> visual
  • loss in the temporal field of one ocular globe + the nasal field of the other ocular globe)
  • Decreased visual acuity
  • Pupillary abnormalities
  • Rarely
  • Optic atrophy
  • Papilledema
  • Cranial nerve palsies
  • The pituitary tumor syndrome-clinical picture
  • Endocrine and metabolic signs and symptoms
  • Hormone hypersecretion (from the adenoma)
  • Hypopituitarism (tumoral local pressure on the healthy pituitary gland or on the
  • hypothalamus)
  • Pituitary stalk syndrome (tumoral compression on the pituitary stalk-> dopamine, releasing
  • hormones and ADH do not reach the pituitary gland->
  • -> lack of inhibition of PRL secretion-> hyperprolactinemia
  • -> hypopituitarism
  • -> diabetes insipidus
  • Pituitary Hypersecretion
  • PRL-
  • - F: amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility
  • - M: ↓ libido, gynecomastia, impotence, infertility
  • GH- syndromes of acromegaly and gigantism
  • ACTH- Cushing disease
  • TSH- hyperthyroidism with goiter
  • FSH, LH- usually without clinical expression but rarely can cause ovarian hyperstimulation

Hypopituitarism #5

  • GH
  • Children: short stature
  • Adults: reduced exercise capacity, ↓ lean body mass, ↑body fat, impaired psychological well-
  • being, ↑ cardiovascular risk
  • LH/FSH
  • F: Oligo/amenorrhea, anovulatory cycles, loss of axillary and pubic hair, osteoporosis
  • M: erectile dysfunction, ↓ libido, testicular atrophy, loss of sexual hair, osteoporosis
  • TSH- hypothyroidism without goiter
  • ACTH- Addison’s disease without hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia
  • Prolactin- failure of lactation
  • ADH- polyuria and polydipsia (diabetes insipidus)
  • Imaging Studies
  • • Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) - High-resolution T1-weighted sections in the coronal and
  • sagittal planes both before and after administration of IV gadolinium= first line method,
  • provides the optimal imaging of the pituitary gland and hypothalamus.
  • - Contraindications: cardiac pacemaker, implanted cardiac defibrillator, metal-containing
  • implants that are not compatible with the MRI
  • • Computed tomography (CT)- for demonstrating calcification in tumors (e.g.
  • craniopharyngiomas) and hyperostosis (meningiomas), bone destruction, hemorrhagic lesions.
  • • Plain skull X rays- may show evidence of pituitary fossa enlargement (however, it does not
  • “see” the pituitary gland or a pituitary tumor) have been superseded by MRI.
  • Management of Pituitary Masses- goals
  • – Excision of mass lesions causing pressure effects
  • – Suppression/correction of hormonal hypersecretion from the tumor
  • – Preserving the normal secretion of anterior pituitary hormones (or correcting their
  • insufficiency)
  • Options: -Surgical treatment
  • - Radiotherapy
  • - Medical treatment
  • The order in which these options are applied depends on the type of tumor, its extension and
  • the response to a previous treatment modality.

Management of Pituitary Masses- options #6

  •  Surgical Treatment
  • 1. Transsphenoidal microsurgical approach to the sella turcica (endoscopically)
  • = is the procedure of choice (with selective resection of the lesion).
  • –– Pituitary microadenoma: complete removal
  • –– Pituitary macroadenoma: partial excision
  • 2. Transfrontal/transparietal craniotomy- rarely- invasive suprasellar mass extending into
  • the frontal/middle cranial fossa/ optic nerves or having extensive posterior clivus
  • invasion.
  • Complications: postoperative hemorrhage, CSF leak, meningitis, visual impairment, transitory
  • diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism.
  •  Radiotherapy
  • It is usually reserved for residual mass effect after surgery when surgery for a compressive
  • mass is contraindicated, or persistent hormone hypersecretion after surgery is noted.
  • 1. Conventional radiation therapy (RT) using high-energy sources (total dose = 10,000–
  • 12,000 Rads in two to three sessions)
  • 2. Gamma knife radiosurgery utilizes stereotactic CT-guided cobalt 60-gamma radiation
  • ->high radiation doses to a narrowly focused area
  • Complications: hypopituitarism, optochiasmatic arachnoiditis, secondary brain tumors.
  •  Medical Treatment
  • • Suppression of hormone hypersecretion
  • 1. Bromocriptine or cabergoline, two dopamine agonists that suppress both PRL and
  • tumor growth in patients with prolactinomas (sometimes used also in nonfunctioning
  • pituitary adenomas)
  • 2. Somatostatin analogues (Octreotide, Lanreotide, Pasireotide)- acromegaly, some TSH-
  • secreting adenomas, Cushing’s disease
  • • Replacement treatment of the anterior pituitary gland insufficiency.
